description: Hello, we are Nava Tavasoli and Jennifer Campbell! We are Canadian undergraduate double-degree electrical engineering students. Nava is also pursuing a degree in computing, and Jennifer is doing a degree in physics as well! We are interesting in the intersection between hardware, software, and the edge of computing and understanding earth science using SI-powered intelligence.
summary: Marcus Crassus, one of the richest Roman leaders in history, is cited as having been the first to ever put together a fire brigade. In his honour, we present Crassus: a spacecraft fire intelligence web application powered by SI to make NASA PSI combustion data research accessible, personalized, and easy to visualize for users. Using 12 TB of available data, it allows users to set experimental conditions and parameters in different environments to visually simulate flames and answer their questions using a RAG-powered chatbot to demystify fire safety in space. It also parses through the data to pull the most relevant fire safety research for a given project, allowing for maximum relevancy searches in a ranking matrix. This is our direct response to the Flame in Freefall challenge, addressing the three fundamental objectives outlined in the proposal. Crassus goes above and beyond by using analytical data to extend the findings of the PSI repository to conditions on Earth.
details:
Crassus is a web dashboard that helps people find and understand spacecraft fire-safety research in NASA’s PSI combustion data. It is built for researchers, subject-matter experts, professors and students. It has three main parts:

  1. Investigation explorer and ranking: It covers all 24 PSI Combustion Science investigations: 19 flown in space (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, ACME, SAME and others) and 5 ground studies. Each is ranked by how much it matters for fire safety in crewed habitats such as the ISS, lunar and Martian bases, and pressurised rovers. Each also shows its tested conditions: oxygen level, pressure, flow and fuel. Users can filter for the conditions future habitats are expected to have, such as at least 30% O₂ at reduced pressure. Hundreds of individual tests are extracted into structured data for flammability modelling, including 262 FLEX droplet tests and 326 spherical-burner tests.
  2. AI research copilot: Users ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn only from the public PSI records. It works as a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline:
    • It finds the most relevant passages using keyword search (BM25) and meaning-based search (embeddings), then merges the two result lists.
    • A large language model writes an answer from those passages.
    • Every claim must cite the dataset’s DOI. Any claim whose citation does not match a retrieved source is dropped before the answer is shown.
  3. Flame visualiser: A real-time WebGL render of how flames behave in microgravity and under electric fields. It uses simplified physics: spherical diffusion flames, jet flame length, and electric-field ion wind. The physics was checked against PSI measurements:
    • Our fitted flame-temperature model matches 324 PSI values to within about 58 K.
    • Droplet burning rates were corrected with a fit to the FLEX data.
    • Anything not yet checked against data is labelled “illustrative”, so model output is never mistaken for measured data.

Because PSI has no public API, we read the JSON backend that powers its website. Records and test-matrix spreadsheets were saved to the GitHub repository once. Their formatting varies widely, so we wrote a separate cleanup script for each investigation with the help of Claude Code. The live app reads only this saved copy, never PSI directly.

Crassus was written using Python, TypeScript, GLSL (WebGL shaders) and HTML. The frontend uses Next.js, React, Motion, Lucide and WebGL2, with components from 21st.dev. The backend uses FastAPI served with Uvicorn, and NumPy for vector search and physics fits. All data is cited to the NASA PSI repository. The frontend physics is tested with Vitest and the backend with pytest. The app is hosted on Vercel. The UI was designed with ChatGPT and Claude Design, then customised by the team.

In building Crassus, we focused on trust and transparency. Answers are limited to cited public records, unverified model output is clearly labelled, and the app does not depend on an undocumented live service.

The aim of Crassus is to make the knowledge in NASA’s PSI repository more accessible for practical applications, and to raise awareness of fire safety in spacecraft. It is also a creative educational tool: by showing how flames look under different conditions, it makes the physics of combustion easier to grasp for users at any level of expertise.
